signal.title: cgroups.procs file of sandbox container is empty. Causing pod deletion to hang since runc can't find the child processes
signal.text: ### Description Encountered this when deploying pods on a node for the first time. When delete the pod like daemonset(`hostNetwork:true` and `hostPID: true`) using `kubectl rollout restart`, pod will get stuck in terminating state(before deletion, pod was in running state) ```sh system nodeconfig-daemon-lqwfh 0/1 Terminating 3 15m 172.16.196.224 mgmt-shuting-md-0-qjdpc-md68p-v22ll <none> <none> ``` Containerd log shows that the container for the pod has been stopped ``` Jun 10 18:39:04 ipv4-tkg252-mc-md-0-bqqjb-x4lb6-ddgj2 containerd[1002]: time="2025-06-10T18:39:04.777342294Z" level=info msg="StopPodSandbox for \"6a854227da6ea4df6d27f45e306df216d14afe8630e00b1c39b65cfccbd0eebf\"" Jun 10 18:39:04 ipv4-tkg252-mc-md-0-bqqjb-x4lb6-ddgj2 containerd[1002]: time="2025-06-10T18:39:04.777464604Z" level=info msg="Container to stop \"6dc8551f393aa08461ec71387b5be6fcfca012275b3f6260232cad3c184fa655\" must be in running or unknown state, current state \"CONTAINER_EXITED\"" ``` But stoping the sandbox container kept reporting `context canceled` ``` Jun 11 03:57:14 ipv4-tkg252-mc-md-0-bqqjb-x4lb6-ddgj2 containerd[1002]: time="2025-06-11T03:57:14.017117303Z" level=error msg="StopPodSandbox for \"6a854227da6ea4df6d27f45e306df216d14afe8630e00b1c39b65cfccbd0eebf\" failed" error="rpc error: code = Canceled desc = failed to stop sandbox container \"6a854227da6ea4df6d27f45e306df216d14afe8630e00b1c39b65cfccbd0eebf\" in \"SANDBOX_READY\" state: wait sandbox container \"6a854227da6ea4df6d27f45e306df216d14afe8630e00b1c39b65cfccbd0eebf\": context canceled" ``` First we are not sure whether containerd reached the containerd-shim successfully, then did a strace on the containerd-shim-runc-v2 that manage the daemonset pod, we found out rpc call did went through, and it was erroring about no child process error, and shim did write reply with "\0\0\0\0\0\0\0\25\2\0" - 10 bytes short RPC string, example like below: ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9c23a453-b324-4dac-ab4b-0d11f0769984) We found out that runc looks for child process in `cgroup.procs` file, and then found out that the cgroup.procs file is **empty**. ``` root@mgmt-shuting-md-0-qjdpc-md68p-ct4nv [ ~ ]# cat /sys/fs/cgroup/devices/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-pod829e9288_6110_40bc_825a_29581aa708b0.slice/cri-containerd-ba20d1c1a8916c0d41dc093295f3786078a58d9c31d736bbdfa52d3359b47e03.scope/cgroup.procs root@mgmt-shuting-md-0-qjdpc-md68p-ct4nv [ ~ ]# ``` `ctr --namespace k8s.io tasks list` still shows the sandbox id and its PID though. But `ctr --namespace k8s.io tasks ps <sandbox-id>` gives empty result. `ps -ax | grep sandbox-PID` could still shows the `/pause` process running **Workaround found** If restarting the containerd, the sandbox container will be recreated, and then new sandbox container cgroups.procs has correct PID. **Other Info** 1.7.23 containerd + 1.1.14 runc + 6.1.141 kernel + cgroupv1 has no issue 1.7.27 containerd + 1.2.5 runc + 6.1.138 kernel + cgroupv1 has issue. We still use cgroupv1 because some vendors still depends on it. Do you know where should we look into that why the content of groups.procs could be empty? Adding debugging log in runc? ### Steps to reproduce the issue 1. 2. 3. ### Describe the results you received and expected The groups.procs should have correct PID when daemonset pods are created ### What version of containerd are you using? 1.7.27 ### Any other relevant information ### Show configuration if it is related to CRI plugin. ``` ## template: jinja # Use config version 2 to enable new configuration fields. # Config file is parsed as version 1 by default. version = 2 imports = ["/etc/containerd/conf.d/*.toml"] [debug] level = "debug" address = "127.0.0.1:6060" [plugins] [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"] sandbox_image = ".../pause:3.9" [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc] runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2" [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc.options] SystemdCgroup = true [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".registry.configs."cas".tls] ca_file = "..." ```

signal.title: Export image config through GRPC service
signal.text: ### What is the problem you're trying to solve In Containerd v1.7 the CRI service status exposed CRI config loaded by Containerd. https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/7f7fdf5fed64eb6a7caf99b3e12efcf9d60e311c/pkg/cri/server/status.go#L68 This config included the registry configuration. https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/7f7fdf5fed64eb6a7caf99b3e12efcf9d60e311c/pkg/cri/config/config.go#L279 During the changes made in #9152 this information was removed to decouple the dependency to the image service. This has removed the ability to verify the configuration currently loaded by Containerd through the CRI API. ### Describe the solution you'd like I would like to find a away to expose the information either through some other API or to consider adding this information back to the current API. Having a look at the current CRI, there is no obvious endpoint where this information could be included. If we were to find another API we would have to find a new endpoint where this would be accessible. ### Additional context Spegel has depended on the ability to check the configuration to be able to verify that Containerd. The latest release of Containerd `v2.0.0-rc.4` has stopped Spegel to work, because it requires configuration verification to work. signal.title: oom: avoid per-wakeup allocations in cgroup v2 OOM watcher (#13558)
signal.text: ## What this does Reduces continuous CPU/GC overhead of the per-container cgroup v2 OOM watcher (`internal/oom`), which is the only steadily-active, workload- proportional code path in `containerd-shim-runc-v2` on a static workload. ## Background (#13558) The watcher arms an inotify `IN_MODIFY` watch on `memory.events`. The kernel notifies that file on **every** counter change (`low`/`high`/`max`/`oom`/ `oom_kill`/`oom_group_kill`), not just OOM kills. Containers running near their memory limit churn `high`/`max` constantly (and increasingly as page cache fills toward the limit over the node's uptime), waking the watcher goroutine very frequently. Previously each wakeup allocated a new read buffer **and** a `map[string]uint64`, then opened and fully parsed `memory.events` with `bufio.Scanner`/`strings.Fields` just to read `oom_kill`. Across ~50–60 shims this steady allocation churn is avoidable CPU and GC pressure that accumulates on long-running nodes. ## Change - Allocate the inotify and `memory.events` read buffers once per watcher and reuse them. - Read only the `oom_kill` counter with a small allocation-light parser. - No behavioral change: OOM detection and cgroup-deletion handling are identical; covered by the existing `TestWatcher` plus a new parser unit test.

signal.title: Update mount manager schema
signal.text: # mount/manager: schema v2, one record per mount ## Issues fixed - **Panic when every mount in a chain is handled by the manager.** `Activate` indexed `mountConv` at `firstSystemMount` to apply a transform to the first mount left for the system to perform; when the whole chain is handled by the manager instead, there is no such mount, `firstSystemMount` equals the chain length, and the index is out of range. Reachable whenever a chain both carries a transform and has a handler registered for its last mount type. Fixed standalone in the first commit. - **Duplicate mounts of an identical filesystem.** `main` has no dedup at all: every activation of the same mount (same image, same options) performs its own independent mount. For a read-only layer that's wasted work; for a shared writable image (e.g. one ext4 block device several containers write into) it's actively corrupting, since two independent read-write mounts of the same filesystem will corrupt it. This change deduplicates and reference-counts identical mounts so there is exactly one real mount no matter how many activations use it. - **Persisted mount state can silently go stale.** `main` decides whether an activation already exists and is usable purely by checking whether a bucket its own bookkeeping wrote is present, never by checking whether the mount it describes is actually still there. A reboot, or an unmount that happens outside this package, leaves that bookkeeping believing a mount exists when it no longer does; on `main` this can surface as `ErrAlreadyExists`, or `Info`, for a mount that isn't really there anymore. This change always checks the mount directly before trusting it, and repairs it in place when it's found to disagree with what's recorded. ## What this does Every mount the manager actually performs is now recorded once, as a "mounted record" (`core/mount/manager/backing.go`), keyed by a digest of its final (post-transform) type/source/target/options. An activation's chain no longer stores mounts inline; each position just points at the mounted record it uses. Two activations that resolve to the same record share it and it stays mounted as long as either uses it; one that can't be shared (e.g. tmpfs) still gets its own record, so there's one code path either way. ## Design points worth flagging for review - **One write transaction per `Activate`, instead of two.** `main` always performs exactly two, regardless of chain length: one to create the activation, and a second, after every mount in the chain is performed, to record the results and mark it complete. This change resolves the whole chain — every position's final mount value and the record it uses — in the first transaction and needs no second one, since mount point and mount time are computed as part of resolving rather than measured afterward. Only possible because `mkfs`/`mkdir` were split into a pure part (computes the resulting mount, safe to run inside a transaction) and an impure part (creates the file/directory, deferred until after the transaction commits). See `rewritePosition` in `transformer.go`. - **Records are never trusted, only checked.** Because mount point and mount time are now computed rather than measured, they can't double as a liveness signal the way `main`'s bookkeeping does, so nothing here relies on persisted state for that: whether a record is actually mounted is always checked directly (`probeMounted` in `manager.go`), via the new `mount.MountedChecker` optional interface if the handler implements it, or the host's mount table otherwise. A record found not to be mounted is repaired in place, reusing its existing id and mount point, rather than minted fresh. - **New public interface: `mount.MountedChecker`** (`core/mount/manager.go`). Optional, type-asserted, same pattern as `metadata.Collector` etc. Needed because a handler's mount point isn't always a real kernel mount — the loopback handler's is a symlink to a device — so a generic mount-table check would always report it as dead. Implemented on `LoopbackHandler` (`core/mount/loopback_handler_linux.go`) via `LOOP_GET_STATUS64`. ## Schema / migration Top level bucket moves from `"v1"` to `"v2"` (structural change, not compatible in place: an old record stores its mount inline, a new one only ever points at a mounted record). `"v1"` is left untouched until this package's first write transaction, which converts it to `"v2"` and deletes it. A rollback to a pre-v2 binary is therefore safe as long as it happens before that first write; not something this store claims to preserve afterward, only to not corrupt. ## Commits 1. `mount/manager: fix panic when every mount is handled by the manager` — small standalone fix, unrelated to the schema change. 2. `mount/manager: move to schema v2, back every mount with one record` — the whole schema/dedup/transaction-count rework described above. ## Testing - Unit and root-requiring tests (`-test.root`) pass at both commits individually, including new tests added: `TestActivateSingleWriteTransaction` (exactly one write transaction per `Activate`), `TestRealizeMountWaitsForConcurrentIdentity` (a second activation blocks on and reuses a mount still being made rather than double-mounting), `TestRealizeMountRepairsInPlace` (same id/path survive a repair), `TestPodGroupSharesOneMount` (N activations, one shared mount). - `-race -count=2` clean on `core/mount/manager`. - `make check`: 24 issues vs. `main`'s own baseline of 25 at the same tip (one fewer, not regressed).

signal.title: [SIG-Node]: KEP-4191: Separate Read and write only layers
signal.text: ### KEP/SIG-Node References - KEP(s): KEP-4191 - stage: beta - KEP Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4191 - KEP PR: see issue link - K8s-Release: 1.31 - KEP-Owner: kannon92 - SIG-Node member liason: kannon92 - KEP-Shepherd: kannon92 Basically this is beta on but there is no containerd implementation for this work. So the feature is in limbo. ### What is the SIG-Node problem you are trying to solve kubelet has two distinct filesystems: Node and Image. In typical deployments, users deploy Kubernetes where both the Node and Image filesystems are on the same disk. There are some requests to separate the storage into separate disks. The most common request is to separate the writable layer from the read-only layer. kubelet and Container data would be stored on the same disk while images would have their own disk. This could be beneficial because images occupy a lot of disk space while the writeable layer is typically smaller. Container IO can impact kubelet and adding the ability for more disks could increase performance of kubelet. However, it is not possible to separate the image layers and container writable layers on different disks. In the current implementation of separate disks, containers and images must be stored on the same disk. So garbage collection, in case of node pressure (really image disk pressure) would GC images/containers on the image filesystem. If one separates writable layer (containers) from readable layer (images), then garbage collection and statistics must account for this separation. Today this could potentially break kubelet if the container runtime configures storage in this way. One downside of the separate disk is that pod data can be written in multiple locations. The writeable layer of a container would go on the image filesystem and volume storage would go to the root fs. There is another request to separate the root and the image filesystem to be writeable and read-only respective. This means that pod data can be written on one disk while the other disk can be read-only. Separting the writeable layer and the read-only layer will achieve this. ### Describe the solution you would like Not really sure on containerd side. ### Additional context I am not able to lead this effort so looking from containerd community. Hope is to unblock the KEP _No response_

signal.title: [SIG-Node]: KEP-5823: Pod-Level Checkpoint/Restore
signal.text: ### KEP/SIG-Node References - KEP(s): KEP-5823 - stage: alpha - KEP Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5823 - KEP PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5851 - K8s-Release: v1.37 (target for Alpha) - KEP-Owner: @rst0git @viktoriaas @adrianreber @andreyvelich - SIG-Node member liason: @haircommander - KEP-Shepherd: TBD ### What is the SIG-Node problem you are trying to solve KEP-5823 introduces native Pod-level checkpoint and restore in Kubernetes, adding `CheckpointPod` and `RestorePod` RPCs to the CRI `RuntimeService`. These RPCs let the kubelet ask a container runtime to: - checkpoint a Pod sandbox and the exact set of selected running containers into a runtime-defined checkpoint format; - restore a new Pod sandbox and its containers from a checkpoint using restore-time sandbox and container configurations; and - pass optional runtime-handler-specific checkpoint and restore options. The initial Alpha proposal focus on two use cases: same-node *warm starts* and *fault tolerance*. The source Pod is temporarily frozen while its state is captured, then resumed after the checkpoint attempt. The checkpoint operation itself does not stop, terminate, or delete the source Pod. The Alpha scope is limited to same-node checkpoint and restore. Cross-node checkpoint transport, live migration, and preservation of device state, volume contents, shared Pod resources, or established TCP connections are deferred to future enhancements. The CRI API was merged in kubernetes/kubernetes#140366. Without a containerd implementation, kubelet calls to these RPCs return `Unimplemented`, and Kubernetes cannot exercise the KEP's end-to-end checkpoint and restore workflow against containerd. ### Describe the solution you would like Implement support for `CheckpointPod` and `RestorePod` CRI v1 in containerd's CRI plugin. The implementation should: - Update the CRI API dependency to a revision containing the merged Pod checkpoint and restore RPCs, and wire them through the CRI service, instrumentation, clients, and test doubles. - Keep the checkpoint format private to containerd and the selected sandbox controller/runtime. Kubernetes treats the checkpoint directory as opaque. - Route checkpoint and restore through an optional sandbox-controller capability so different sandboxers can provide their own implementation and unsupported controllers can return `Unimplemented`. For `CheckpointPod`: - Validate the request, caller deadline, output directory, sandbox, and selected container IDs. - Require every selected container to belong to the requested sandbox and be running, and reject duplicate or incomplete selections. - Quiesce the selected Pod containers as one coordinated transaction. - Capture the sandbox configuration, container configurations and statuses, writable filesystem layers, and runtime checkpoint state beneath `output_path`. - Keep the source Pod running after either success or failure. - Honor cancellation and gRPC deadlines, remove partial artifacts on failure, and publish only a complete checkpoint. - Reject unsupported runtime-specific options rather than silently ignoring them. For `RestorePod`: - Treat `checkpoint_path` as read-only and validate the checkpoint before changing containerd state. - Select the requested runtime handler and reject incompatible or unsupported checkpoints. - Create a new sandbox using the supplied `PodSandboxConfig`. - Match the supplied `ContainerConfig` entries to checkpointed containers by container name. - Restore checkpoint-owned process and filesystem state while applying compatible restore-time settings such as mounts, resources, logging paths, labels, annotations, devices, and security constraints. - Return the new sandbox ID and an exact name-to-container-ID mapping for the restored containers in `CREATED` state so the normal CRI lifecycle can start them. - Preserve normal containerd runtime selection, metadata stores, cleanup, event, and NRI behavior. ### Additional context Relevant links: - WG Checkpoint Restore: https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/main/wg-checkpoint-restore - Meeting notes: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ZMtHBibXfTw4cQerM4O4DJonzVs3W7Hp2K5ml6pTufs/edit

signal.title: Proposal: Support Pod-level checkpoint and restore
signal.text: ### What is the problem you're trying to solve Hello, maintainers, This issue proposes the containerd architecture and tracks implementation work for KEP-5823. It distinguishes the intended containerd contract from the current Kata Containers/QEMU prototype. The Sandbox API remains open for review. ## KEP References > First of all, Thanks the KEP owners bring us such amazing feature! - KEP: [KEP-5823: Pod-Level Checkpoint/Restore](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/5823-pod-level-checkpoint-restore) - CRI API proto: https://github.com/kubernetes/cri-api/blob/release-1.37/pkg/apis/runtime/v1/api.proto - Kubernetes release: v1.37 - KEP owners: @rst0git, @viktoriaas, @adrianreber, @andreyvelich - SIG-Node liaison: TBD - KEP shepherd: TBD ## Problem KEP-5823 adds `CheckpointPod` and `RestorePod` to CRI. containerd needs to coordinate these Pod-level operations with sandbox runtimes. Independent container checkpoints cannot capture a consistent VM or shared sandbox. The sandbox runtime must own the Pod-wide execution-state boundary, while containerd must continue to own CRI validation, lifecycle locking, CNI, NRI, new IDs, task adoption, publication, rollback, and restart recovery. ### Describe the solution you'd like ## Proposed solution Split responsibility as follows: - kubelet performs Kubernetes validation, allocates the checkpoint directory, sets the deadline, and starts restored containers; - containerd coordinates host-side CRI resources and the restore transaction; - the sandbox runtime captures and restores opaque runtime state. Pod C/R is optional per sandboxer and runtime handler. Unsupported handlers return an explicit unsupported error. Runtime-specific artifact formats remain opaque to containerd. The initial reference profile is: ```text sandboxer: shim runtime: Kata Containers VMM: QEMU network: CNI with new network identity rootfs: runtime-owned NRI: staged restore when enabled ``` The initial scope excludes `sandboxer="podsandbox"`, runc Pod-level C/R, live migration, preserved Pod IP, cross-node transfer, generic external Volume/Device restore, and a universal checkpoint format. ### Checkpoint ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant K as Kubelet participant C as containerd CRI participant S as Sandbox controller participant R as Sandbox runtime K->>C: CheckpointPod(request, deadline) C->>C: Validate and lock source sandbox C->>S: Checkpoint(sandbox ID, task inventory, path) S->>R: CheckpointSandbox R->>R: Pause all tasks and capture one Pod-wide checkpoint R->>R: Resume all tasks before returning R-->>S: Result S-->>C: Result C->>C: Unlock source sandbox C-->>K: Response or causal error ``` The runtime handles partial-artifact cleanup and task resumption within the same checkpoint call. containerd does not issue a separate resume RPC. ### Restore ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant K as Kubelet participant C as containerd CRI participant D as Durable and CRI stores participant N as CNI and netns participant S as Sandbox controller participant R as Sandbox runtime participant I as NRI participant T as Task manager K->>C: RestorePod(request, deadline) C->>C: Validate, allocate new IDs, and lock C->>D: Persist Restoring marker C->>N: Create netns and run CNI alt NRI enabled C->>S: PrepareRestore S->>R: Restore sandbox without task records C->>I: Run sandbox and container hooks C->>T: PrepareRestoredTask C->>S: CompleteRestore S->>R: Restore task records without running processes else NRI disabled C->>T: PrepareRestoredTask C->>S: RestoreSandbox S->>R: Restore sandbox and task records end R-->>S: Controller and exact task inventory S-->>C: Restore result C->>C: Validate inventory C->>T: AdoptRestoredTask C->>D: Persist RestoredCreated C->>D: Publish Ready sandbox and CREATED containers C->>D: Clear restore transaction C-->>K: New sandbox and container IDs K->>C: StartContainer ``` Restore is transactional. On failure, containerd rolls resources back in reverse order. It deletes the durable marker last; if cleanup is incomplete, it keeps the marker so restart recovery can retry. The initial rootfs profile is runtime-owned. The sandbox runtime restores the writable layer, and containerd does not create a replacement snapshot. This is a profile-specific behavior, not a requirement for every runtime. ## Alternatives and extensibility We considered these alternatives: - independent container checkpoints do not provide a consistent VM or sandbox checkpoint; - interpreting checkpoint formats in containerd would couple CRI to individual runtimes; - delegating the whole operation to the runtime would bypass containerd-owned CNI, NRI, metadata, task, and rollback semantics; - skipping NRI would make restored workloads differ from normally created workloads; - always creating a new snapshot can replace checkpoint-authoritative writable state for a runtime-owned-rootfs implementation. The design separates CRI orchestration, sandbox-controller capabilities, and runtime-specific implementation. These boundaries can survive package changes inside containerd and allow future sandboxers, rootfs profiles, and restore protocols without adding Kata/QEMU-specific logic to the common CRI path. ## API decision The prototype adds `CheckpointSandbox` and `RestoreSandbox` to the existing Sandbox service. A separate optional C/R service is another viable design. Extending the existing service avoids another registration path but may affect source compatibility for regenerated third-party shim interfaces. A separate service preserves the existing generated interface but requires additional registration and discovery. Maintainer feedback is required before the API or the staged-restore transport is considered final. ### Additional context ## Draft implementation and evidence To make the design concrete and facilitate code-level discussion, an exploratory implementation is available as a Draft PR: [Draft pod-level C/R in containerd ](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/x) . It is provided as feasibility evidence and review context, not as a final API or merge-ready implementation. The API shape and patch structure are expected to change based on maintainer feedback. - And the reference Kata/QEMU implementation is available at [Pod-level C/R in Kata-Containers/Sandbox API](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/pull/13654). It is provided as a reference implementation for the sandboxer="shim" profile, not as a final Kata/QEMU implementation. The Kata/QEMU implementation is expected to change based on maintainer feedback. - And the reference rust-extensions implementation is available at [rust-extensions with pod-level C/R](https://github.com/Apokleos/rust-extensions/tree/ckpt-restore). ## Feedback requested 1. Should Pod C/R extend the existing Sandbox service or use a separate optional service? 2. Is `sandboxer="shim"` with Kata/QEMU an acceptable first reference implementation? 3. Any other feedbacks ? After these decisions, the implementation can be submitted as a reviewable PR series covering the Sandbox API, task adoption, CRI/CNI orchestration, staged NRI restore, rollback/recovery, and tests. Looking forward to your feedback. Appreciate it!

signal.title: metadata: bound snapshotter Remove during garbage collection
signal.text:
Fixes #13798 **Problem** During snapshot GC, `cleanupSnapshotter` calls the snapshotter's `Remove` while holding the metadata store write lock, with no deadline (it even strips the caller's cancellation). If the snapshotter never answers, the lock is held forever. Every snapshot operation on the node queues behind it, including CRI `RunPodSandbox`, so no new container can start. Nothing on the readiness path takes this lock, so the node keeps reporting Ready the whole time. ```mermaid flowchart TD K[kubelet] -->|Ready probe| S["CRI Status()"] K -->|RunPodSandbox| P[snapshot Prepare] S --> OK["returns OK - never takes the lock"] P --> L{{metadata store write lock}} GC[snapshot GC] -->|holds| L GC -->|"Remove() - no deadline"| SOCI[soci snapshotter
out of fds, never answers] L -.->|blocked behind GC| P ``` We hit this in production: our soci snapshotter ran out of file descriptors and stopped answering, the GC's `Remove` parked in `waitOnHeader`, and the node could not start a single pod for 4.5 hours while showing Ready. Goroutine dumps are in the issue. The fd leak was a soci bug (fixed upstream in awslabs/soci-snapshotter#2043), but any proxy snapshotter that stalls reproduces this: one stuck RPC should not brick the node. **Fix** Bound each GC-path `Remove` with a `pkg/timeout` key (`io.containerd.timeout.snapshot.remove`, default 5m), the same pattern as shim cleanup and bolt open timeouts. On the first timed-out `Remove` the rest of the pass is abandoned, so a wedged snapshotter costs one timeout per GC cycle instead of one per orphan. Skipped snapshots stay orphaned and are retried next pass. The deferred `Cleanup` call is skipped in that case too, since it is an unbounded RPC to the same snapshotter that just failed to answer. **Not in this PR** `Walk` runs under the same lock and is also unbounded. Left out to keep this change small; can follow up.

signal.title: cri: use the platform configured in runtime_platforms
signal.text: # cri: use the platform configured in `runtime_platforms` ## Motivation Developer clusters increasingly run on arm64 hosts, for instance, an Apple Silicon laptop running a KinD node, or an arm64 CI runner, while a large amount of software is still published as `linux/amd64` only. Today the node's platform is the only platform containerd will pull for, so such an image fails with `no match for platform in manifest` and the workload is simply not runnable, **even though the host can execute amd64 binaries perfectly well through Rosetta or `qemu-user-static`**. The only workaround is to rewrite the `architecture` field in each image's config and side-load the result, which is invasive, has to be redone per image and per tag, and falsifies image metadata. containerd already has the config surface to do this properly. `runtime_platforms` maps a CRI runtime handler to an `ImagePlatform{Platform, Snapshotter}`, but only `Snapshotter` is ever read: the platform is parsed by the plugin, stored on the image service, and never consulted. This PR reads it. ```toml [plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.images".runtime_platforms."runc-amd64"] platform = "linux/amd64" ``` ```yaml spec: runtimeClassName: runc-amd64 # -> images pulled and unpacked as linux/amd64 ``` The node stays arm64, so the kubelet, etcd and containerd keep running natively and nothing about the node changes; only images for pods that opt into the `RuntimeClass` are selected for another platform. ## Relationship to prior work This is the sibling of the already merged [#12710](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/12710), which made `PullImage` honor the `runtimeHandler` parameter and pick a snapshotter from `runtime_platforms`. It left the `Platform` field of the same struct unused. This PR reads it, on the same code path, with the same opt-in and the same config surface: no new config, no new API field, no change to how images are keyed. It is intentionally narrower than the KEP-4216 series ([#9832](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/9832) → [#10533](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/10533) → [#11807](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/11807)), which aimed to make an image a `(reference, platform)` tuple so the same reference can exist for two platforms at once. That requires changes to `core/images`, the image store schema, GC labels, `RemoveImage` and the reload path. This PR does not attempt it and does not conflict with it — the platform matcher list added to the CRI image store is the natural place for that work to land, and carries the `TODO`. ## Changes * `image_pull.go`: `snapshotterFromPodSandboxConfig` becomes `imagePlatformFromPodSandboxConfig`, resolving snapshotter **and** platform for the runtime handler. The platform is passed to `client.Pull` `WithPlatformMatcher`) and to the transfer service (`WithPlatforms`/`WithUnpack`), and used to resolve the config descriptor of the pulled image. * `internal/cri/store/image`: the store holds a list of platform matchers instead of one, tried in order, resolving an image against the first whose content is present locally. Without this, an image pulled for a configured platform is invisible to `ImageStatus` and `ListImages` and the kubelet loops on the pull. * `check.go`: image reload accepts any configured platform, so images pulled for one are recovered on restart rather than dropped. * `helpers.go` / `opts/container.go`: `toContainerdImage` carries the platform the image store resolved, so snapshot creation and the unpack fallback on container creation use the same platform as the pull. * `docs/cri/config.md`: `runtime_platforms` was undocumented; adds a worked example and the caveats. An unset `platform` behaves exactly as before: the platform of the node is always the first matcher, so the default path is unchanged. The first commit is an independent fix to the v2 → v3 migration of this same field, which wrote it under `runtime_platform`, read the v2 snapshotter from `snapshot` instead of `snapshotter`, and stored a `platforms.MatchComparer` where a platform string is expected. ## Requires the `RuntimeClassInImageCriApi` kubelet feature gate Like #12710, this depends on the kubelet populating `ImageSpec.RuntimeHandler` in `PullImageRequest`. That is gated behind `RuntimeClassInImageCriApi`, alpha and off by default as of Kubernetes 1.35. With the gate off, `runtimeHandler` is empty and behavior is unchanged. ## Design points for review **Node architecture labeling.** The node keeps advertising `kubernetes.io/arch=<native>` while running foreign-architecture images, so the scheduler and architecture-based `nodeAffinity` are unaware. Relabelling the node would be wrong, since the kubelet and containerd themselves still run natively. The boundary is that this is opt-in per `RuntimeClass`: nothing changes unless an admin both configures a handler with a platform and creates a `RuntimeClass` for it. It targets emulation-capable hosts — Rosetta, or `qemu-user-static` registered with the binfmt `F` flag so it applies in nested container namespaces. containerd selects the image; it does not provide the emulation. **Pinned images and the sandbox image.** These stay on the platform of the node even when the handler asks for another one: they are shared by every pod and are part of containerd's own infrastructure. This is asymmetric with the snapshotter, which *is* overridden for pinned images — existing behavior I left alone, since the sandbox rootfs has to live in the runtime's snapshotter. Happy to revisit if reviewers prefer symmetry. **Inheritance between handlers.** Not implemented. An unset `platform` means the platform of the node, which is what the existing doc comment on `ImagePlatform` says and the only reading that keeps the default path untouched. Inheriting across handlers would make the meaning of one handler depend on unrelated entries in the map. **Known limitation.** A reference resolves to one platform at a time. If the same reference is pulled both for the platform of the node and for a configured platform, `ImageStatus` and `ListImages` report the one matching the node. Removing this is exactly the `(reference, platform)` keying the KEP-4216 series was after. ## Testing Unit tests alongside the existing snapshotter-selection tests: * `TestImagePlatformFromPodSandboxConfig` — platform and snapshotter resolution, the deprecated annotation fallback, unset platform, pinned images staying native. * `TestImagePlatformMatchers` — ordering (node platform first) and deduplication. * `TestStoreResolvesNonDefaultPlatform` — a multi-platform index whose content is present for only one platform: not resolvable with the node matcher alone, resolvable once the configured platform is added, node platform still preferred when both are present. * `TestRuntimePlatformsConfigMigration` — the migration fix. signal.title: cri: report swap and pod-level IO PSI in CRI stats
signal.text: The CRI stats path never filled `ContainerStats.Swap`. A kubelet running with the `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` feature gate therefore reports no container swap, and no pod swap either, because the kubelet aggregates pod swap from container stats. The sandbox metrics path already reads swap from cgroups to emit `container_memory_swap`, so the data was available and just not mapped into the stats response. This change adds a `swapContainerStats` helper and wires it into `linuxContainerMetrics`: - cgroup v1: `memory.memsw.*` accounts memory and swap combined, so the swap-only usage is memsw usage minus memory usage, and the swap limit is memsw limit minus memory limit. When the memsw files are missing (swap accounting disabled), stats collected with `IgnoreNotExist` leave a zeroed `Swap` entry. A real memsw limit is never zero, so a zero limit is treated as swap stats unavailable and nothing is reported. - cgroup v2: `memory.swap.*` accounts swap only and is used directly. `SwapAvailableBytes` is only set when a real swap limit is configured. This matches the kubelet's cadvisor-based swap accounting (`cadvisorInfoToSwapStats`). `ListPodSandboxStats` also never set `LinuxPodSandboxStats.Io`, while the per-container path already reported IO pressure (PSI) through the shared `ioContainerStats` helper. The sandbox path now calls the same helper. The pod sandbox cgroup collection also includes `StatIO` now, so `io.pressure` is actually read. `StatCPU` and `StatMemory` already include their pressure files. Both fixes close gaps in KEP-2371 (kubernetes/enhancements#2371) parity for the `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` feature gate, which is targeting beta in Kubernetes 1.37. The kubelet consumes these fields in its strict CRI stats path (`pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go`, swap aggregation in `addSwapStats` and pod PSI in `addCRIPodIOStats`). One related issue is left out of scope on purpose. On cgroup v1 the metrics path (`list_pod_sandbox_metrics_linux.go`) emits `container_memory_swap` from the raw `Memory.Swap.Usage` value, which is memsw and therefore includes memory usage. cadvisor subtracts memory usage there. That looks like a separate bug and can be fixed in a follow-up if maintainers agree. Unit tests cover both cgroup versions, including the memsw arithmetic, the unlimited and zero swap limit cases, and the zeroed swap entry case when swap accounting is disabled.

signal.title: Mount OCI Artifacts
signal.text: ### What is the problem you're trying to solve Hi, In containerd, supporting mounting OCI Images is currently under review (#10579). However, according to: [Guidelines for OCI Artifact Usage](https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/blob/main/manifest.md#guidelines-for-artifact-usage), it is allowed to use customized media types beyond application/vnd.oci.image.layer.v1.tar. https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4639, it seems that OCI Artifacts are intended to be valid VolumeSources for mounting in Kubernetes. At this time, I assume that containerd does not support general OCI artifacts at this time (even after #10579). **NOTE for matainers**: This is actually a different topic from a related issue (#10285), which primarily addresses choosing a container runtime based on artifact type. What we want is for containerd to support pulling and mounting OCI Artifacts, which is independent of runtime selection. That's why we created this dedicated issue to discuss this topic. We've raised a similar issue in cri-o as well (https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/issues/8953). **Background**: We are currently working on a [spec for AI/ML models as OCI artifacts](https://github.com/CloudNativeAI/model-spec/blob/main/docs/spec.md) aimed at efficiently delivering models to Kubernetes. We've defined several custom media types at different levels: - For *layer*: `application/vnd.cnai.model.layer.v1.tar`, `application/vnd.cnai.doc.layer.v1.tar`, etc. - For *manifest*: `application/vnd.cnai.model.manifest.v1+json` - For *config*: `application/vnd.cnai.model.config.v1+json` Currently, we prefer to use our custom-defined media type for *config* instead of `application/vnd.oci.image.config.v1+json` because we think this might be a more idiomatic usage of OCI artifacts. However, **we also have some concerns about things like `diff_ids`**. See (issue https://github.com/CloudNativeAI/model-spec/issues/22) for details. We are interested in understanding the plans of container runtime like containerd regarding support for generic OCI artifacts, which would facilitate our next steps. Thank you! ### Describe the solution you'd like support pulling and mouting OCI artifacts. ### Additional context _No response_

signal.title: New k8s CRI API: image_id in PullImageResponse
signal.text: ### What is the problem you're trying to solve The `PullImageResponse` message of the Kubernetes CRI API was updated to include `image_id`, which is designed to formalize the image identifier across CRI API messages. This means that the value of image identifier fields across different CRI API messages MUST always be the same as long as it refers to the same image. See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137217 for more information on the affected fields. ### Describe the solution you'd like Include `image_id` in CRI API's `PullImageResponse` ### Additional context This change happened because we recently identified that the `image_ref` field was not filling the role of a unique image ID properly due to its vague definition. Even though in containerd this works fine, we would like to make sure we have a stable identifier that we can use for each container runtime. This does not mean that identifiers must be the same across all runtimes - the stable identifier rule only applies within each of the runtimes.

KEP-6061 adds an `OCI` profile type to the Kubernetes API and a `PullSecurityProfileArtifact` RPC to the CRI `ImageService`, enabling the kubelet to pull profiles via the runtime using existing registry infrastructure and credentials. ### Describe the solution you would like containerd needs to implement the `PullSecurityProfileArtifact` RPC on `ImageService`. signal.title: [SIG-Node]: KEP-5474 - Enable Writable cgroups for unprivileged containers
signal.text: ### KEP/SIG-Node References - **KEP(s):** [KEP-5474](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5475) - **Stage:** Alpha - **KEP Issue:** [kubernetes/enhancements#5474](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5474) - **KEP PR:** [kubernetes/enhancements#5475](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5475) - **K8s-Release:** v1.38 (Target for Alpha) - **KEP-Owner:** @Divya063 - **SIG-Node member liaison:** TBD - **KEP-Shepherd:** @chrishenzie (Volunteering) ### What is the SIG-Node problem you are trying to solve KEP-5474 proposes a mechanism to allow unprivileged containers to have write access to their cgroup filesystem (`/sys/fs/cgroup`) on cgroup v2 systems. Currently, this is only possible by running a container in privileged mode, which poses a security risk. This feature is required for several use cases, including running nested containers (Docker-in-Docker) and allowing applications to perform fine-grained, in-process resource management for their child processes. This issue is to track the implementation of the required CRI changes in containerd to support this KEP. ### Describe the solution you would like As proposed in the KEP, the containerd CRI implementation needs to be updated to support a new `writable_cgroups` field in the `LinuxContainerSecurityContext` message of the CRI API ```protobuf message LinuxContainerSecurityContext { // ... existing fields ... // writable_cgroups controls whether the container has write access to cgroup interfaces. // Only effective with cgroup v2. bool writable_cgroups = 18; } ``` When this field is set to `true`, containerd should mount `/sys/fs/cgroup` as read-write for the container. This behavior should be conditional on the host system using cgroup v2. This new CRI field will supersede the existing [`cgroup_writable`](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/6ab42082fdddb01bec445ba141daeb53198dbd61/docs/cri/config.md?plain=1#L289) configuration option in the runtime config for Kubernetes workloads. ### Additional context **Timeline and Release Coordination:** A primary point of discussion for this KEP is the release schedule coordination between Kubernetes and containerd, as [raised in this KEP review comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5475#discussion_r2291880771). The KEP targets Beta in v1.36, which requires a released version of a container runtime with this feature implemented. - The CRI API changes will be part of the Kubernetes v1.35 release (est. December 2025). - The next containerd minor release (2.2) is scheduled for November 2025, which is *before* the Kubernetes v1.35 release. This creates a dependency issue where containerd would need to depend on a pre-release version of the CRI API to include this feature in the 2.2 release. This issue will be used to track the feasibility of this approach and coordinate the implementation and release plan to ensure the KEP can meet its graduation criteria. **Related Issues:** - Previous containerd discussion: [#10924](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/10924) - Corresponding Kubernetes issue: [#121190](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/121190) mikebrow: moved the release target to k8s 1.38 due to KEP stats

signal.title: [SIG-Node]: 5758 - Per-container ulimits configuration
signal.text: ### KEP/SIG-Node References - KEP(s): KEP-5758 - Per-container ulimits configuration - https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/5758-per-container-ulimits-configuration - stage: alpha - KEP Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5758 - KEP PR: - https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5762 - https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/6157 - K8s-Release: v1.38 - KEP-Owner: @HirazawaUi - SIG-Node member liason: TBD - KEP-Shepherd: @HirazawaUi ### What is the SIG-Node problem you are trying to solve KEP-5758 adds Kubernetes API and CRI support for configuring POSIX resource limits on a per-container basis. Today, Kubernetes users cannot set ulimits directly in a Pod spec. Containers inherit runtime or host defaults, which makes workloads that need specific limits, such as `nofile`, `memlock`, `core`, `nice`, `rtprio`, or `stack`, depend on node-level runtime configuration or entrypoint-level workarounds. This is not portable and is hard to manage in multi-tenant clusters. The KEP proposes adding `securityContext.ulimits` to containers and passing those values through CRI via `LinuxContainerSecurityContext.ulimits`. containerd needs corresponding CRI implementation work so kubelet can create containers with the requested limits. The KEP also needs runtime feature discovery so kubelet / node-declared-features can determine whether the runtime supports per-container ulimits before scheduling Pods that request them. ### Describe the solution you would like Implement containerd CRI support for KEP-5758: - Accept the new CRI `LinuxContainerSecurityContext.ulimits` field when creating Linux containers. - Validate / translate CRI ulimit entries into OCI runtime spec `Process.Rlimits`. - Preserve existing behavior when no ulimits are specified. - Handle `-1` values according to the KEP: map them to the effective runtime / kernel unlimited value where applicable, with runtime-side clamping where needed to avoid invalid `setrlimit(2)` calls. - Expose runtime support through CRI `RuntimeFeatures`, so kubelet can advertise node support through node-declared-features. ### Additional context _No response_ @mikebrow : moved target to k8s v1.38 target given status in KEP

signal.title: pkg/sys: add actionable hint to socket dir permission errors
signal.text: Motivation: On macOS (and other non-root deployments), containerd can fail at startup with a bare "mkdir /var/run/containerd: permission denied" even when root, state, and [grpc] address are all set to custom, writable paths (containerd/containerd#12444). This happens because the grpc and ttrpc server plugins each carry their own hardcoded default socket address under /var/run (or /run), independent of the configured root/state/[grpc] address. A user who only overrides [grpc] address still hits the hardcoded ttrpc default (or a misconfigured debug address), and the resulting permission-denied error gives no indication of what to change. Approach: This does not change any default address. Doing so would require a way to distinguish "address left at its hardcoded default" from "user explicitly set this value" at plugin config-decode time, which the current plugin config model does not support, and is a larger, design-level change than fits a surgical fix. Instead, pkg/sys.mkdirAs — the single chokepoint used by the grpc, ttrpc, and debug server plugins via GetLocalListener — now wraps a permission-denied error from creating the socket directory with a hint identifying the grpc/ttrpc hardcoded default and telling the user to configure a writable address for the grpc, ttrpc, and debug plugins. This is a diagnostics-only change: the exact command from the issue will still fail on a non-root user with an unwritable default state dir, but the error now explains why and what to do, instead of a bare "permission denied". Validation: go build ./... go test ./pkg/sys/... -v Added TestMkdirAsPermissionErrorIncludesHint, which reproduces a non-root permission-denied mkdir (via a 0500 parent dir) and asserts the wrapped error still satisfies errors.Is(err, os.ErrPermission) and includes the new hint text. Both commands pass on darwin/arm64. Updates #12444 Signed-off-by: Pujitha Paladugu <10557236+pujitha24@users.noreply.github.com>

signal.title: runtime/v2: shim delete can fail before exec when the bundle directory has been removed
signal.text: ### Description core/runtime/v2.(*binary).Delete() starts a shim binary for the delete action. On Linux, it currently sets the shim process cwd to the bundle path: WorkDir: b.bundle.Path pkg/shim/util.go then applies it directly: cmd.Dir = config.WorkDir If a create failure/timeout rollback removes the bundle before this best-effort delete path runs, the shim delete command can fail before the shim binary starts: fork/exec /path/to/containerd-shim-xxx-v2: no such file or directory The error is misleading because the shim binary exists; the missing path is the configured working directory. Expected: The shim delete action should still be startable even if the original bundle directory has already been removed.
